title: Indian-American Woman Falsely Accused of Visa Fraud in Viral Post, US Attorney Steps In
excerpt: A Houston biomedical engineer and Kuchipudi dancer was branded a visa fraudster on X. The US Attorney for Southern Texas confirmed she is a naturalized citizen.
body:
• Sadhana Gollapudi, a biomedical engineer and Kuchipudi dancer in Houston, was falsely accused of student visa fraud on X by an anonymous account
  • US Attorney Aaron Reitz confirmed she is a naturalized American citizen, not on a student visa
  • The episode highlights a growing pattern of misinformation targeting Indian-origin individuals in the US

An Indian-origin woman in Houston, Texas, became the target of a viral misinformation campaign after an anonymous X account accused her of exploiting the student visa system — claims that a US federal official directly debunked.

Sadhana Gollapudi, a biomedical engineer who also performs Kuchipudi, a classical Indian dance form, was singled out in a July 30 post by an account operating under the handle "CyberGreen09." The post branded her a "forever F1 student since 2014" and accused her of "playing the student visa game" for 12 years by enrolling in multiple programs. A video of Gollapudi performing Kuchipudi was attached alongside the claims, with the hashtag #visafraud.

US Attorney Debunks the Claims

As the post gained traction, Aaron Reitz, the US Attorney for the Southern District of Texas, intervened directly on August 4.

"My office looked. She's a naturalized US citizen, not here on student visa. As US Atty over Houston, I take visa fraud seriously. We prosecute it to the fullest."

— Aaron Reitz, US Attorney for the Southern District of Texas

Reitz's confirmation dismantled the central claim in the viral post. Gollapudi is not on a student visa — she holds full American citizenship.

Gollapudi Speaks Out

On August 6, Gollapudi broke her silence on Instagram, describing the ordeal as "incredibly difficult and upsetting" for both her and her family.

"My content has been reposted without my permission on another social media platform by an account that is spreading false and misleading claims about me," she wrote, urging followers to report the posts for misinformation. "Your support means more than you know."

Questions About the Source

The account behind the claims raised its own red flags. The bio of CyberGreen09 describes it as a "fan account" of Pakistani actor Hamza Sohail. Following backlash, the account was made private. Multiple users accused the profile of being a troll account with a history of pushing anti-India content.

The Indian American Advocacy Council weighed in on X, criticizing the response dynamics. "An American woman was filmed, named and falsely branded a 'visa fraudster' before millions," the group wrote, noting that while the US Attorney cleared Gollapudi's name, he "used her exoneration to rant about 'illegal aliens' and who is 'welcome on American soil.'"

A Broader Pattern

The episode is not isolated. Research by the Network Contagion Research Institute found that anti-Indian rhetoric on X nearly tripled between 2024 and 2025, with roughly 24,000 explicitly anti-Indian posts generating over 300 million views. Just three accounts produced 525 posts that drove 20 percent of all reposts in the dataset.

In Texas, camera-wielding YouTubers have built a content niche around doorstepping Indian immigrants at their homes and businesses, accusing them of H-1B fraud. Immigration lawyers who reviewed the footage found no violations established in any of the confrontations.

The broader climate has been shaped by the $100,000 H-1B petition fee introduced by the current administration and escalating anti-India rhetoric from political figures, which researchers say has given lower-level influencers a template to localize.

What It Means for the Diaspora

The Gollapudi case crystallizes a growing fear among Indian-Americans: that any visible expression of Indian identity — a dance performance, a business listing, an accent — can be weaponized into a viral accusation. The fact that a US Attorney had to personally intervene to debunk a single social media post underscores both the reach of this misinformation and the institutional resources required to counter it.

For Indian-Americans navigating an increasingly hostile online environment, the case is a reminder that documentation and community support remain the most effective defenses. Civil rights organizations including the South Asian Bar Association now accept incident reports from those targeted by similar campaigns.
nri_angle: Indian-American woman in Houston targeted by anti-India misinformation campaign, highlighting rising online hostility toward the diaspora.
author: Diaspora Desk
